To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
utopias, dystopias, and their hybrids can be understood as particular cybernetic information systems in which human minds are the system’s nodes and in which data is stored, processed, and exchanged.
utopias, dystopias and the future societies they envision can be understood as particular types of cybernetic systems that process and transmit information.

utopias, dystopias, and posthuman neuropolities are cybernetic information systems that are expected to be realized in the near future, and which can be studied using the model we present in this paper.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether and how the emergence of neuropolitical societies will change our ability to envision and realize utopias and, if so, how such societies might be envisioned in works of audio-visual science fiction.
the ways in which the development of cybernetic technologies for human enhancement will affect our ability to create and inhabit utopias and/or dystopias.
the following questions: How do utopias and/or dystopias function as cybernetic information systems?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
utopias, as a concept, are not only a way for people to imagine the perfect society, but also a way of understanding how people think and act in the world.
the future of utopias is in the hands of the people, and it is up to them to decide whether they want to create a better society or a society that is more dystopian.
this article is about how the future is going to be and what it will look like.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown how utopias and dys-topias can be understood as particular types of information systems, and we have argued that the advent of neuroprosthetics will allow (or even compel) the creation of novel kinds of utopian and dystopian information systems.

the human brain and mind are the most complex cybernetic information systems in the world and that the human mind is capable of creating utopias and/or dystopias as cybernetic information processing systems.
we are interested in the ways in which utopia/dystopia can be understood as a cybernetic information system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
utopias are not necessarily better than dystopias and that the former should not be seen as a panacea for all of the ills of the present-day world.
it is possible to envision the posthuman future as an emerging information system in which the minds of human and posthuman beings are connected to one another to form a new type of society.
utopias, dystopias, and their hybrid forms are not only sociopolitical constructs, but they can also be understood in terms of the cybernetic information systems that they are.
